title: Kubernetes vs Docker Compose
description: Kubernetes is the stronger default when production workloads need multi-node resilience, autoscaling, and orchestration across failure domains, while Docker Compose is the stronger default when the deployment target is single-node, the operational budget is small, and development parity matters most. The decision is usually about whether you need a control plane that continuously reconciles desired state or a lightweight service graph on one host.
name: Kubernetes vs Docker Compose
problem: The engineering decision is whether to deploy AI/ML serving, training, or data platform workloads on Kubernetes or Docker Compose, where the real trade-off is resilience and scale versus operational simplicity and minimal overhead. Kubernetes is designed for large-scale cluster management and continuous reconciliation, while Docker Compose is designed for declarative multi-container application execution on a single Docker engine.

evaluation_criteria.description: Horizontal scaling, auto-healing, and fault tolerance.
Control plane overhead and per-workload resource utilization.
Helm charts, Operators, service mesh, and CI/CD integration.
Local development parity and deployment iteration speed.
Infrastructure, personnel, and managed service costs.

options.name: Kubernetes
strengths: Production-grade auto-healing, rolling updates, and rollback.
Horizontal pod autoscaling and cluster autoscaling.
Declarative state management with desired state reconciliation.
weaknesses: Steep learning curve and significant platform engineering investment.
Version upgrade complexity and API deprecation.
options.best_for: Multi-node production workloads, microservices, auto-scaling serving, complex stateful apps.
options.avoid_when: Single-node deployments, small teams without platform engineers, or rapid prototyping.
infrastructure_required: Control plane nodes or managed control plane.
Worker node pool with container runtime.
failure_modes: etcd quorum loss causing cluster unavailability.
CNI misconfiguration causing pod network isolation.
OOMKilled cascades from resource limit misconfiguration.
Control plane overload from excessive API server requests.
Image pull failures due to registry or secret issues.
hidden_costs: etcd storage growth and backup infrastructure.

options.name: Docker Compose
strengths: Extreme simplicity and minimal operational overhead.
Declarative YAML with intuitive service dependency graph.
Easy CI/CD integration for simple deployments.
weaknesses: Manual failover and no built-in load balancing.
No resource scheduling or placement control.
Limited secrets management and network isolation.
options.best_for: Local development, single-node production, prototypes, small teams, CI/CD pipelines.
options.avoid_when: Multi-node scaling, high availability requirements, or production workloads requiring auto-healing.
infrastructure_required: Optional reverse proxy for multi-service routing.
failure_modes: Single host failure causing total service outage.
No automatic restart on container crash unless configured.
Resource contention between services on shared host.
Storage volume corruption without distributed replication.
Manual intervention required for topology changes.
hidden_costs: Downtime during updates and configuration changes.

comparison_table.Architecture: Kubernetes: Distributed control plane plus workers | Docker Compose: Single-node Docker daemon
comparison_table.Scaling: Kubernetes: Horizontal across pods and nodes | Docker Compose: Vertical only on one host
comparison_table.Auto-Healing: Kubernetes: Native | Docker Compose: None by default
comparison_table.Rolling Updates: Kubernetes: Native | Docker Compose: Manual recreation
comparison_table.Resource Overhead: Kubernetes: Control plane and cluster services | Docker Compose: Negligible
comparison_table.Operational Team: Kubernetes: Platform or SRE team | Docker Compose: Small generalist team
comparison_table.Multi-Cloud: Kubernetes: Native portability | Docker Compose: Not applicable
comparison_table.Service Discovery: Kubernetes: Cluster DNS and networking | Docker Compose: Docker network DNS
comparison_table.Storage: Kubernetes: CSI plugins and dynamic provisioning | Docker Compose: Docker volumes and bind mounts
comparison_table.Networking: Kubernetes: CNI plugins and policies | Docker Compose: Bridge networks and port mapping
comparison_table.Local Development: Kubernetes: Kind, minikube, or k3d | Docker Compose: Native docker compose up

recommendations: Choose Kubernetes for production multi-node AI serving, training orchestration, and resilient data platform deployments. Choose Docker Compose for local development, single-node production, and early-stage systems where platform overhead is unjustified. Use Depends when the near-term need is rapid delivery, but the product roadmap likely crosses into multi-node availability or autoscaling.
use_cases: Production model serving fleet: Kubernetes with HPA and GPU node pools.
Local LLM development environment: Docker Compose for rapid iteration.
Multi-tenant SaaS platform: Kubernetes with namespace isolation.
Data science notebook deployment: Docker Compose for single-user instances.
Real-time inference pipeline: Kubernetes with autoscaling.
CI/CD test environment: Docker Compose for ephemeral integration tests.
Edge device deployment: Docker Compose on single-board computers.
Training job orchestration: Kubernetes with batch schedulers and cluster autoscaling.
one_sentence_summary: Kubernetes is the stronger default when production workloads need multi-node resilience, autoscaling, and orchestration across failure domains; Docker Compose is the stronger default when the deployment target is single-node, the operational budget is small, and development parity matters most.
choose_when: Kubernetes: Production multi-node serving, high availability requirement, complex microservices topology, GPU workload scheduling, or multi-cloud/hybrid deployment | Docker Compose: Single-node prototype or MVP, small team with < 5 engineers, local development environment, or budget-constrained startup.
avoid_when: Kubernetes: Single-node deployments, small teams without platform engineers, or rapid prototyping | Docker Compose: Multi-node scaling, high availability requirements, or production workloads requiring auto-healing.
hybrid_recommendation: Use Docker Compose for local development and CI/CD integration tests while production runs on Kubernetes, keeping Compose files as the developer-facing source of truth and maintaining Kubernetes manifests separately.
assumptions: You have containerized applications such as model serving, training jobs, or data pipelines.
You have infrastructure resources such as cloud VMs, bare metal, or managed services.
You have engineering capacity for platform operations.
Deployment targets range from single-node to multi-cluster.
scope: This guide compares Kubernetes and Docker Compose for container deployment. It covers orchestration, scaling, networking, storage, and operational characteristics.
out_of_scope: Serverless deployment as the primary comparison.

common_mistakes: Using Docker Compose for production multi-node workloads.
Underestimating Kubernetes operational complexity and team requirements.
Not planning the Docker Compose to Kubernetes migration path early.
Ignoring resource limits in Kubernetes and creating noisy-neighbor behavior.
Assuming Docker Compose production parity without volume and backup planning.
Over-engineering with service mesh before proving the need.
Not using managed Kubernetes to reduce control plane burden.

decision_tree.question: Do you need multi-node deployment or high availability?
Do you have dedicated platform or SRE engineering capacity?
Is this for local development or single-node production?

hybrid_strategy.when_both_wins: Use Docker Compose for local development and CI/CD integration tests while production runs on Kubernetes. This is the common pattern when teams want developer ergonomics without sacrificing production resilience.
hybrid_strategy.architecture_overview: Use Docker Compose for local development and CI/CD integration tests. Use Kubernetes for staging and production environments. Keep Compose files as the developer-facing source of truth and generate or maintain Kubernetes manifests separately where needed.
benefits: Fast local iteration with Docker Compose.
Shared service definitions for development workflows.
CI/CD can test against Compose before Kubernetes deployment.
costs: Potential drift between development and production behavior.

migration_path.description: Docker Compose for development and initial production.
Traffic growth, availability requirements, and team capacity.
Services incrementally from Compose to Kubernetes.
Docker Compose for local development parity.
